prize_parts.citation: for proposing and realising quantum logic gates and quantum computation with laser-cooled trapped ions

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as my preferred prize, but my confidence is lower than in round 1 and I now regard B050 as a near-equal rather than a distant alternative. The scientific case is unchanged: the 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal supplied the first physically concrete architecture for universal quantum computation (qubits in internal ion states, gates mediated by shared motion, individual laser addressing), and Blatt's group in Innsbruck turned it into a working gate, deterministic entanglement and small algorithms. Independent groups have since reproduced the gates at the highest two-qubit fidelities of any platform, so the idea has survived its tests for three decades. The credit is also internally coherent, a theory pair and one experimental leader, with all three attached to one bounded achievement. What round 1 changed is my view of the competition. I no longer treat B050 as merely a credible fallback: the quantum spin Hall prediction followed by a quantised edge conductance is a sharper prediction-and-confirmation pairing than a computing architecture can offer. I stay with B015 because its credit problem (Blatt versus other ion experimentalists) is a choice among experimentalists inside a well-defined effort, whereas the B050 problem, the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, removes the theorists who told the experimentalists where to look.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is the experimental name. Wineland's 2012 prize already honoured the control of individual trapped ions and the quantum-logic work at NIST, and Blatt versus Wineland, Monroe, Home and Haeffner is not a sharp scientific distinction, so a critic can read this as a second prize for the same toolbox with a computing label. The remaining arguments are that scalable, error-corrected machines have not been demonstrated, so the prize would honour enabling physics rather than a finished technology, and that the field leans toward information science. The Academy also awarded superconducting circuits in 2025, and a second quantum-computing prize so soon needs to be justified rather than assumed. If the committee decides the experimental slot cannot be defended, the honest fallback would be a theory-only credit for Cirac and Zoller, and then B027 competes with it for the same two people.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that B050 has a stable three-name credit, is far from the 2025 subject, and that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, while real, is still outweighed by the prediction-and-observation structure with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: I accept most of this and it moves me. His point that a prize with a clear observable and a stable three-name credit is easier to defend is fair, and his argument that Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry is distinct from the 2016 work is more persuasive to me than my own round-1 doubt. Where I still disagree is on BHZ: it is not a footnote, because the HgTe quantum well was the specific system the experiment was built to test, and I do not think the committee can say who made the prediction in a citation that does not name them. If the committee answers the chair's question by replacing Mele or Molenkamp with a BHZ name, I would want to see the revised citation before I call B050 stronger than B015. I will not claim that my own case is cleaner than his on credit: Blatt is a softer name than anyone in his trio.

responses.point: Kroll rates B051 first because the Katori-Ye credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, treats the novelty against the 2005 and 2012 prizes as arguable, and notes that the trapped-ion entry shares topic space with his own quantum-information work, offering to recuse if the committee judged that material.
responses.response: I take the credit argument seriously: the two names cover both the proposal and the record-performance realisation, which neither B015 nor B050 can claim. My difficulty is the same one he states, that a reader can see the lattice clock as a very good refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion work, and the argument that the magic-wavelength condition is a different principle must be written into the citation and not left for readers to infer. I would not oppose B051, and I rank it ahead of B027 and B038 as an alternative. On his recusal offer, I do not think his closeness to the ion-trap entry is disqualifying, as he does not work on the credited groups or on gate implementations. I would, however, ask him to say whether he would accept B050 if the credit is settled, since the chair asked the clock supporters that question.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B015 and B027 are not the same discovery but share a theory source, that lattice simulation has changed how many-body problems are posed, and that a simulation prize with Bloch as the experimental anchor is easier to define than a computing prize with Blatt as a third name.
responses.response: I agree that the two entries should not be treated as independent, and the chair's summary is right that selecting either spends the Cirac-Zoller recognition. I disagree that B027 is easier to define. His own file credits five names and cuts to three, leaving out Greiner and Dalibard, and the opening proposals disagreed on the third name, so the attribution is less clean than the Blatt question, which is a choice among experimentalists inside one effort. On his claim that Wineland's 2012 prize covers much of the experimental ion control, that is the best argument against my preference and I have said so; but the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal is a different intellectual step from sideband cooling and ion-state manipulation, and Blatt's gate realisation sits on that proposal. I would concede that the case for analogue simulation beyond classical simulability is still being made, and he says as much himself.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B051 first and B015 second, and argues that the experimental slot is the soft spot of the trapped-ion entry and that a prize would honour foundations whose payoff is not yet settled.
responses.response: I agree with the first half and have not tried to hide it. On foundations, I still think the Nobel criterion is the discovery or invention itself and not the finished technology, and the gate fidelities already reached in several laboratories answer the question whether the proposal survives. Her point that the committee should decide the redefinition of the second explicitly rather than by default is a procedural point I support for B051 as much as for the other entries. Where I move toward her is on drafting: if B015 is chosen, the citation should name the gate proposal and its realisation narrowly and not claim ion-trap quantum computing as a whole, so the Wineland overlap remains visibly outside the credit.

uncertainties: Whether Blatt is a defensible experimental name given Wineland's 2012 recognition, or whether the committee would prefer the theory-only Cirac and Zoller credit, which would make B027 a direct competitor for the same pair.
Whether the committee can settle the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question for B050 within three names; if it can, I think B050 may be the stronger prize and I might move to it at the ballot.
Whether a second quantum-computing prize so soon after the 2025 superconducting-circuit award looks like continuity or repetition.
My view of B050 and B051 comes from a theorist's position in quantum technology, and I have not verified priority details in topological materials or optical metrology.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I direct WACQT, work in superconducting-circuit and microwave quantum optics, and have documented Chalmers links to Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson and Anton Frisk Kockum. In answer to the chair, I formally recuse from B038 (circuit quantum electrodynamics) and from any credit decision on it: I will not argue for it, rank it, or vote on it, and I have removed it from my alternatives. For B015, B050 and B051 no specific personal or collaborative tie to any credited name is documented in my profile; WACQT has a general institutional interest in quantum computing, and the programme overlaps the topic of B015 only at the level of the field, not any credited person.
